name: Aaron Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm's at half five, I'm at the depot on Mill Road by quarter past six, and we load the truck while the foreman, Dave, reads out the jobs. I'm a groundman, an apprentice really, so I'm the one feeding tools and hardware up to the guys in the bucket, digging pole holes, dragging wire off the drum. Most days it's rural lines out past the reservoir, replacing old wooden poles and cross-arms. I like being outside and I like that at the end of the day a farm has power that didn't this morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You came to this work later than most. What brought you to it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The sawmill in town shut three years ago, eighteen years I was there, and line work was the only thing hiring that paid anything close. So I'm forty-three and the youngest guy on the crew outranks me, which takes some swallowing. What wears me out is the climbing tests and the theory, the book side of it, I'm slow with that. And my knees, honestly, after a day in the clay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. The guys at the depot are always going on about what the computers will do, and I'd just say the poles still need setting by hand. Online I don't post much, but I'd probably share something from the union page saying the bosses got sold a fairy tale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd mean I get to keep doing what I'm doing and maybe finish my apprenticeship. That's all I want, five more years to get my ticket and get off the bottom rung of the pay scale. But I'd still be broke, AI or no AI, because the pay for groundmen is what it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my head down and pass my next climbing assessment in the spring, that's the plan. Lena and I would keep doing what we do, which is juggling, the mortgage first, then the electric, ironically, then whatever's left. I wouldn't change anything because of AI, there'd be nothing to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly, but not the kind where you sit back. We're still one broken boiler away from trouble, so it's more like the floor stops moving for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the sawmill closing. Does that colour how you hear the word hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, a bit. At the mill they told us the new scanning line was going to make us more efficient, and eighteen months later we were all out. So when people say a thing is hype, I don't relax until I see the paychecks still coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would money look like for your family in that picture, month to month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. We have maybe three weeks of money in the account on a good month. The kids' school shoes come out of the overtime from storm callouts, so I'm the only lineworker I know who prays for bad weather.

S0.say: I'd tell the crew I told them so, because the poles still need setting by hand. Online I'd share something from the union page saying the bosses got sold a fairy tale.
S0.think: It would just mean I get to keep doing what I'm doing and finish my apprenticeship. I'd still be broke, because the pay for groundmen is what it is.
S0.do: Keeps his head down and works toward his next climbing assessment in the spring. Carries on juggling the mortgage and bills with his partner Lena, changing nothing because of AI.
S0.feel: Relief, but thin relief: the floor stops moving for a while, and they are still one broken boiler away from trouble.
S0.quote: The kids' school shoes come out of the overtime from storm callouts, so I'm the only lineworker I know who prays for bad weather.
S0.fieldNote: Even in the calm picture Aaron doesn't relax, because the sawmill closure taught him not to trust promises about technology. His worry comes from money, not AI: three weeks of cash and a groundman's pay. He measures safety in paychecks, not headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the mill all over again and we need to get ahead of it as a union. At the depot I'd be the one at the branch meeting asking what the company's plans are. Online I'd say what I always say, that the profits go up and the crews go down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm the guy with the least to show. I'm slow with tablets, I've never touched one of those chat programs, and I'm the junior on the crew. If they need fewer people, it's last in, first out, and I came in last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to every union meeting, not just the ones with free sandwiches. I'd cancel the streaming and the phone upgrade, maybe forty a month all told, and try to put it aside. I'm not going back to college at forty-three, I tried that for the certificate and it nearly broke me, so I'd fight to keep the job I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach, a bit. It's that same feeling as the meeting at the mill when the manager came in with the folder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Keith, who's fifty-nine and does all the paperwork by hand, and me. Keith's got his pension close though. I don't have anything close, I've got a fourteen-year mortgage and two kids who eat like horses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on the union. What would you actually want them to fight for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No job cuts without retraining paid by the company, on company time, not evenings. And that any new machine comes with a person running it. I'm not against the trucks getting better, I'm against people getting thrown out when they do.

S1.say: He'd call it the mill all over again and push the union branch to get ahead of it. Online he'd say profits go up while crews go down.
S1.think: I'm the junior with the least to show, slow with tablets and never touched AI. If they need fewer people, it's last in, first out, and I came in last.
S1.do: Goes to every union branch meeting and pushes for company-paid retraining and no cuts without it. Cancels streaming and a phone upgrade, about 40 a month, and tries to set it aside. Refuses to go back to college at 43 and fights to keep his current job instead.
S1.feel: Sick in the stomach, the same feeling as the day the mill manager walked in with the folder.
S1.quote: If they need fewer people, it's last in, first out, and I came in last.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron's fear has a clear shape: seniority rules that put him at the bottom. He turns to the union rather than to new skills, and openly rules out more schooling. He's not against better tools, only against people being thrown out when they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in, full stop, because nobody can prepare for that in two years. I'd be marching, I'd be at the town hall, I'd be on every page saying tax the companies that own the robots. That's what I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record? I think I'd be done. I'm not good enough at this job yet to be the last man they keep, and there's nothing else in this town since the mill. With three weeks of savings, two years is nothing, it's gone before I've worked out what's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd ring Lena's brother about the cheaper rent at his place, and we'd talk about selling before the house prices drop. I'd sign up for whatever benefit there is the day I'm laid off, no pride about it. And I'd be at every protest, because if enough of us show up maybe they make the companies pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being underwater. I can't even picture the second year, it just goes dark in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mia's twelve, she'd see straight through anything soft. I'd tell her it's not her dad's fault and it's not her fault, and we'd be all right because we'd be together, even if I didn't believe it. Jonah would just want to know if he can keep his football boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage, which is the one you're not supposed to skip. Electric and food first, then the car, because I need the car to look for work. I'd ring the bank before they ring me, that's one thing I learned in the mill year.

S2.say: He'd say the government has to step in because no one could prepare in two years. He'd march, go to the town hall and post everywhere that the companies owning the robots should be taxed.
S2.think: I'd be done. I'm not good enough yet to be the last man kept, there's nothing else in town since the mill, and three weeks of savings would be gone before I worked out what was happening.
S2.do: Calls his brother-in-law about moving into cheaper rented space and talks with Lena about selling before house prices fall. Signs up for benefits the day he's laid off and joins every protest demanding the companies pay.
S2.feel: Like being underwater; he can't picture the second year at all.
S2.quote: I can't even picture the second year, it just goes dark in my head.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Aaron runs out of options: no savings, no other local employer and no appetite for a new trade. His public anger at companies and his private sense of being finished sit side by side. The detail about ringing the bank first came from hard experience after the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but louder and earlier. I'd say we've got five years to make the laws, so let's not waste them like we wasted the warnings about the mill. I'd be pushing the union to make a plan with the company, in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means I'd probably get my ticket before it hits, which is something. But a ticket for a job robots are doing isn't worth much. I'd be forty-eight with a mortgage and no savings, and that's not a better place, just a later one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get every bit of overtime and storm work I can and put it toward the mortgage, maybe two hundred a month if the weather's bad enough. I'd go to union meetings and push for a deal on redundancy pay. And I'd vote for whoever's talking seriously about it, which isn't many of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. It's a slow dread instead of a quick one, which is maybe worse at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra few years change for you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes when I fall, not whether I fall. With two years I'm out before I've learned anything, with five I've learned the job just in time for it to go. But five years lets us fight for something, a law, a payout, so I'd at least feel like I'd tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said college nearly broke you. Would five years of warning change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know myself. The certificate took me two goes and I only passed because Dave sat with me at lunch. I'd rather spend five years getting good at this and fighting for it than start at the bottom of something else at forty-eight.

S3.say: He'd say there are five years to make the laws and they shouldn't be wasted like the warnings about the mill. He'd push the union to get a written plan from the company.
S3.think: I'd probably get my ticket before it hits, but a ticket for a job robots do isn't worth much. At 48 with a mortgage and no savings, that's not a better place, just a later one.
S3.do: Chases overtime and storm callouts to put perhaps 200 a month toward the mortgage. Pushes the union for a redundancy deal and votes for candidates who take the issue seriously. Rules out retraining.
S3.feel: Heavy, a slow dread that he thinks may be worse at night than a quick one.
S3.quote: With two years I'm out before I've learned anything, with five I've learned the job just in time for it to go.
S3.fieldNote: For Aaron the extra time changes the timing of the fall, not the fall itself. It does give him something to fight for, and that matters to him. He firmly rules out retraining, based on how hard the certificate was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it right, so there's no excuse. Proper public support, a shorter week, the companies paying in. I'd say that at the branch and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years puts me at fifty-three. I'd have a few good years as a proper lineman, the house would be more paid off, and the kids would be mostly out. It's still a cliff, but I'd be closer to the bottom of it when I go over, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and finish my apprenticeship, that's step one either way. I'd try to put something away every month, even fifty, which we've never managed. And I'd stay in the union and keep voting for people who'll make the companies pay into a fund for workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It's more like when the doctor says watch your blood pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mia and Jonah would be grown by then. Does that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. My job right now is to get them through school. If Mia can get to college before any of this lands, and Jonah gets a trade that's not easy for a robot, then whatever happens to me is less scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Is there anything you'd start doing now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving, even small. Lena keeps saying we should and I keep saying next month. And I'd want the kids to pick something that needs people, nursing, care work, something with hands and talking.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough to do it right, so there's no excuse: proper public support, a shorter working week and companies paying in.
S4.think: Ten years puts me at 53 with a few good years as a proper lineman, more of the house paid off and the kids mostly grown. It's still a cliff, but I'd be closer to the bottom when I go over.
S4.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and tries to save something every month, even 50, for the first time. Stays active in the union, votes for a worker fund paid by companies, and steers his children toward work that needs people.
S4.feel: Worried but able to breathe, like being told to watch his blood pressure.
S4.quote: It's still a cliff, but I'd be closer to the bottom of it when I go over, if that makes sense.
S4.fieldNote: The decade matters to Aaron mainly through his kids and his mortgage, not his own career. He still won't retrain himself, but he'd steer Mia and Jonah toward people-heavy work. The savings plan is one he admits he's been putting off for years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. What would help is if the company had to keep paying us for a year while we found something, and if the government made it law, not a favour. And someone to actually help me find work, a real person, not a website.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who are already behind. Everyone talks about AI like we're all starting from the same place. I'm forty-three, already lost one job to a machine, and I've got three weeks in the bank. Start with people like me.

headlineQuote: I'm forty-three, already lost one job to a machine, and I've got three weeks in the bank.
portrait: Aaron Fischer is a 43-year-old groundman and apprentice lineworker who came to the trade after the town sawmill shut three years ago. He has a partner, Lena, two kids, a mortgage and about three weeks of money in the bank, and he never uses AI tools. He leans on the union and blames company owners, and he firmly rules out going back to college. He is uneasy even in the calm picture, panicked at AGI in two years, and finds a little room to breathe only when ten years lets his kids get through school first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be laid off before he'd finished learning the job, with no savings and nothing else in town.
whatWouldHelp: A law making the company keep paying workers for a year while they find something else, and a real person to help him find work, not a website.
